title: Asking questions
topic: three ways to ask: intonation, est-ce que, inversion (fixed phrases); question words
why: This lesson teaches you to ask questions the way the French really do: with intonation, with est-ce que, and with a few fixed inverted phrases, plus all the question words and quel in its four forms. Now you can not only introduce yourself but also get to know someone.

Yes or no? Three ways to ask

English builds questions with “do” and by swapping words: “Do you live in Paris?”, “Are you French?”. French has three ways, from the most relaxed to the most formal.

wayexampleregister
1. Rising intonationTu habites à Paris ?everyday speech, the most common
2. Est-ce que + statementEst-ce que tu habites à Paris ?neutral, spoken and written
3. Inversion (verb-subject)Habites-tu à Paris ?formal, written

Intonation is the simplest: take a normal sentence and raise your voice at the end. Est-ce que (literally “is it that”) is a question marker placed in front of an ordinary sentence; it becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel: Est-ce qu'elle parle anglais ?

Inversion is studied much later. For now, learn just a few fixed phrases that use it:

Comment allez-vous ?How are you? (formal)
Comment vous appelez-vous ?What's your name? (formal)
Quel âge as-tu ?How old are you? (to a friend)

Answering a negative question: si

To contradict a negative question, French doesn't say oui but si:

Tu ne parles pas français ? — Si, je parle français !Don't you speak French? — Yes, I do!

In writing, French puts a space before ? and ! (and before : and ;): Tu es anglais ? Never “anglais?” glued to the word.

", "

Question words

To ask for information, you need a question word. Here are the essential ones:

FrenchEnglishexample
quiwhoQui est le professeur ?
qu'est-ce que / quoiwhatQu'est-ce que tu regardes ? / Tu regardes quoi ?
oùwhereOù est la gare ?
d'oùwhere… fromVous êtes d'où ?
quandwhenTu arrives quand ?
commenthowTu t'appelles comment ?
pourquoi → parce quewhy → becausePourquoi ? — Parce que j'aime Paris.
combien (de)how much, how manyTu parles combien de langues ?

Where does the question word go?

In everyday speech, the French love to put it at the end, in the place of the missing information: Tu habites où ?, Tu t'appelles comment ?. In more careful French, it goes first, followed by est-ce que: Où est-ce que tu habites ?, Comment est-ce que tu t'appelles ?. Both are correct.

“What” has two forms: qu'est-ce que at the start, quoi at the end: Qu'est-ce que tu cherches ? = Tu cherches quoi ? Never put quoi first in this kind of question.

Watch the accent: où (where) vs ou (or). Tu habites où ? but Tu travailles ou tu étudies ?

", "

Quel, quelle, quels, quelles

Quel means “which” or “what” in front of a noun, and like everything in French, it agrees with the noun. The four forms sound exactly the same: only the spelling changes.

singularplural
masculineQuel âge as-tu ?Quels livres est-ce que tu aimes ?
feminineQuelle est ton adresse ?Quelles langues est-ce que tu parles ?

With être, quel agrees with the noun that follows: Quelle est ton adresse ? (l'adresse is feminine). Take ton (your) as part of the phrase for now: possessives come in unit 5.

Getting to know someone

Here are the questions you'll ask and hear all the time. Notice the tu and vous versions:

  • Tu t'appelles comment ? / Comment vous appelez-vous ?
  • Tu habites où ? / Où est-ce que vous habitez ?
  • Tu es d'où ? / Vous êtes d'où ?
  • Quel âge as-tu ? / Tu as quel âge ?
  • Pourquoi est-ce que tu étudies le français ? — Parce que j'aime la France.

And to return the question, just say Et toi ? (to a friend) or Et vous ? (formal): take them as fixed phrases.

Tu parles combien de langues ? — Trois. Et toi ?How many languages do you speak? — Three. And you?

Combien needs de (or d') before a noun: combien de langues, combien d'amis. No article after it: never “combien des langues”.
